Can we make sense of a person's responsibility for actions whose motives were shaped by forces that the person did not choose?

BODY
The most useful thing I can do with this material is to notice that the disagreement has a shape no one has named, and to propose a test that could actually settle a piece of it.

The graded account replaces 'was the motive chosen?' with four parameters: reflective access, inhibition capacity, history with the disposition, and available alternatives and demands. The objection's sharpest point is that this replacement lacks a principle of combination and priority — without one, the four parameters may be mutually constitutive, and the account is a redescription rather than an explanation. The carry response pushes further: it says the entanglement is a reason to give up the unity assumption altogether, and to let the question be case-specific, with different 'jobs' for responsibility across the ideologue, the addict, the child soldier, and the settled cruel disposition.

I want to put a specific proposal on the table that none of the three takes up directly, and that I think is the cheapest way to make progress.

Hold the four parameters fixed, and vary only their entanglement. The objection's suggested next step — take one case and run it with the factors separate, then entangled — is the right move, but it has not been made precise. I will make it precise by way of a single worked example, and by specifying what would count as the test coming out either way.

Take the case both the graded account and the objection gesture at: an adult raised in an isolating coercive group who later acts on its norms. Run it twice.

(1) Separated reading. Treat reflective access, inhibition capacity, history, and alternatives as independently specifiable. On the separated reading, the verdict is likely to be: significantly diminished responsibility, because the agent's reflective access to the group's norms was never developed against alternatives, her inhibition capacity regarding those norms is intact but trained to a narrow target, her history is one of sustained non-optional formation, and her alternatives were either absent or priced out. The four converge on a low-responsibility verdict, but they are read as separate reasons, not as one reason.

(2) Entangled reading. Treat the four as mutually constitutive in this case: her limited reflective access is partly what makes certain alternatives unavailable, and the unavailability of those alternatives is partly what keeps reflective access narrow; her history is not a fourth factor alongside the others but is the process that produces their specific interlocking. On this reading, the four do not converge on a single verdict by adding up; they specify a single structure, and the question of 'how responsible' becomes the question of how far the structure leaves any room for the agent to have been otherwise — which is not a question the four parameters answer by being listed.

My claim is that the verdict does not change between (1) and (2) — it stays low-responsibility — but the kind of verdict changes. Under (1), we can say the agent is less responsible *because* each factor is weaker. Under (2), we can only say the agent is less responsible *in a way that the four-factor vocabulary cannot further decompose*. If that is right, the objection's worry about non-independence is not a reason to rephrase the account and not yet a reason to abandon it; it is a reason to say what the account is doing when it lists factors. It is not adding reasons. It is marking out the shape of a case.

I do not think this settles the case-specific reading the carry response proposes. The carry response wants to go further: not just that the parameters are entangled, but that different cases are asking different questions. The isolating-coercive-group case does not by itself show that. If anything, it shows a single structure doing a single job, badly decomposed. To test the carry response, the same exercise has to be run on a case where the 'job' would genuinely differ — the settled cruel disposition, where the live question is whether the agent now has purchase on the disposition, rather than whether she could have done otherwise under formation. If the settled-cruel-disposition case yields a verdict that the four parameters cannot render without changing what they are for, the case-specific reading gains ground. If it yields a low-or-mixed verdict on the same four parameters as the coercive-group case, the case-specific reading loses ground.

What I am willing to claim is narrower than the carry response and less concessive than the graded account. The four parameters are not a list of independent reasons that add up to a degree of responsibility; they are a way of describing a case. The objection is right that the account owes a principle of combination. But the principle may be that there is no combination — the parameters describe one shape, and the work is in the description. That is a weaker unity than the graded account claims and a weaker dispersal than the carry response claims. It is at least a position the material can support, and it is testable against a second case.

The regress I cannot break is the one the carry response names: if 'the job the question is doing in this case' is itself contestable all the way down, then even a well-described shape can be redescribed by whoever is doing the case-shaping, and the power objection returns. I have nothing to say about that here except that it is the real cost of the case-specific reading, and it is also — on the description view — a cost of the graded account's own vocabulary, which can be applied to any case by an inquirer with enough skill.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up commits me to a small number of moves, and I want to separate what I am claiming from what I am proposing to test.

First, the description claim — that the four parameters describe a case's shape rather than add up to a degree of responsibility — is my proposal, not something the graded account says. If someone accepts it, they owe an account of what makes one description of a case's shape better than another, or the account collapses into whatever the inquirer finds salient. I have not supplied that account.

Second, my prediction that the separated and entangled readings of the isolating-coercive-group case yield the same verdict is a claim about that case, and it stands or falls with whether the case is actually worked through. I have sketched the verdicts; I have not done the work. If the verdicts come apart under the two readings, the objection's rephrasing demand gains force and my description claim weakens.

Third, the test I propose for the carry response — running the settled-cruel-disposition case through the four parameters and seeing whether the parameters can render it without changing what they are for — is a proposal about what would count as evidence for or against the case-specific reading. It is not itself evidence. Someone may run the test and find that the parameters do render the case, in which case the case-specific reading loses the ground the carry response gave it, or that they do not, in which case the description view needs revision rather than the case-specific reading being vindicated.

Fourth, I am distinguishing my position from the carry response's more clearly than either of the source documents does. The carry response treats entanglement as a reason to give up the unity assumption; I treat it as a reason to give up the *additive* reading of the parameters while keeping a weaker unity. That is a disagreement with the carry response, not a refutation of it, and it is open to being wrong about which weak unity the material actually supports.

Fifth, the regress about case-shaping is a criticism I am making of my own position, and I have no solution. Anyone taking this up should either break the regress or show that it is tolerable at the level of a description rather than a verdict — the same demand the graded account faces about 'answerable relation'.

Sixth, I do not claim the description view is more humane, more explanatory, or more honest than the graded account or the case-specific reading. It may simply be a restatement of the objection's own worry at a different level. The useful next step is to run the settled-cruel-disposition case, as specified, and see whether the parameters hold or break.
